name: BM25 and Relevance Ranking
intent: Rank matching documents by how well they fit the query, scoring each query word by how rare it is, how often it appears (with diminishing returns) and how long the document is.
scenario: A shop search has found the pages that mention the words of the query "cheap laptop battery". The test corpus is 8 short pages, 99 words in all, from a 2-word page to a 40-word review. One page is keyword-stuffed: 18 words, 14 of them "laptop". Sorting by how many times the query words appear puts that page first, with a score of 15 against 3 for the real best match. The team needs a score that rewards a page about the topic, not a page that repeats the word.
problem: Finding the documents that contain the words is the easy half. Ordering them is where raw counts fail. A long document repeats words by accident of length, so it beats a short, focused one. A common word such as "the" appears everywhere and tells you nothing, but it adds to the count as much as a rare word. And the 10th occurrence of a word says far less than the 2nd: a page is about laptops after a few mentions, and more mentions are padding. Anyone who knows the rule can exploit it by stuffing keywords. A good ranking function has to stop all three.

howItWorks.title: Start from counts, and see why they fail
howItWorks.text: The simplest score is the sum of term frequencies (tf): how many times each query word occurs in the document. It ranks the 40-word review above the 6-word guide for "the laptop battery" only because "the" occurs 10 times in the review, and it ranks the keyword-stuffed page first because it has 14 occurrences. The count grows without limit, ignores how common a word is across the corpus, and ignores how long the document is. Each of the next three steps fixes one of those.

howItWorks.title: Inverse document frequency: rare words say more
howItWorks.text: Inverse document frequency (idf) weights a word by how few documents contain it. With N documents and df of them containing the word, a common form is idf = ln(1 + (N - df + 0.5) / (df + 0.5)), the one Lucene-based engines use. In the 8-page corpus "battery" is in 4 pages and "cheap" in 3, so "cheap" is worth more per match; a word in every document would be worth almost nothing. Plain TF-IDF multiplies tf by idf. That fixes the "the" problem, but tf still grows in a straight line, so the stuffed page still wins with 13.16.

howItWorks.title: Saturation: the 10th occurrence adds less than the 2nd
howItWorks.text: BM25 replaces raw tf with tf x (k1 + 1) / (tf + k1). With k1 = 1.2 and a document of average length, one occurrence is worth 1.00, two are worth 1.38, ten are worth 1.96 and twenty only 2.08: the curve flattens toward k1 + 1 = 2.20 and never passes it. The parameter k1 sets how fast it flattens. At k1 = 0 a word is either present or not; at a large k1 the weight stays close to a straight line for longer. Fourteen repeats of one word now buy about twice what a single mention does, not fourteen times as much.

howItWorks.title: Length normalization: a long document gets less credit per word
howItWorks.text: A long document has more chances to contain any word, so its counts are discounted. BM25 divides by tf + k1 x (1 - b + b x length / average length). The parameter b runs from 0 (ignore length) to 1 (full correction). With b = 0.75 the stuffed page, at 18 words against an average of about 12, is held back and falls to number 3. With b = 0 it climbs back to number 2; with b = 1 a 2-word page that says only "cheap laptop" takes the top spot, so full correction over-rewards short documents. Common defaults in Lucene-based engines are k1 = 1.2 and b = 0.75.

howItWorks.title: The score is a sum, and the parameters are tuned, not guessed
howItWorks.text: The BM25 score of a document is the sum over query words of idf x saturated tf x length factor. It needs only numbers the index already stores: df per term, tf per posting, the length of each document and the average length. It is a heuristic, so k1 and b are worth tuning on your own data against judged queries (see Search Quality Evaluation) instead of trusting any default. Production ranking often puts BM25 first as a cheap candidate generator, then re-ranks the top few hundred with a learned model.

pros: Needs only statistics an inverted index already keeps, so it is cheap to compute at query time
Resists keyword stuffing and long-document bias with two documented parameters
Rare words count for more, common words almost nothing, with no stop-word list needed
A strong baseline that is hard to beat by much without labeled data and a learned ranker
cons: Knows only word statistics, not meaning: a synonym or a paraphrase scores zero
k1 and b interact with your data and need tuning; the defaults are a guess about someone else's corpus
Scores from different queries or different indexes cannot be compared with each other
Treats every field alike unless you weight fields yourself, so a title match and a footer match count the same
whenToUse: Keyword search over documents of very different lengths, such as product pages, articles or tickets
A first-stage ranker that picks candidates for a heavier re-ranking model
Any search that needs a sound, explainable ranking before there is click or judgment data
whenNotToUse: Matching by meaning across different wording, where embeddings and vector search fit better
Short fields of equal length (names, tags), where length normalization adds nothing and an exact or boolean match is enough
Ordering by a business rule such as price, date or distance, which is a sort, not a relevance score
pitfalls: Setting b to 0 or 1 to simplify: 0 lets long pages win by length, 1 favors tiny pages
Comparing BM25 scores across queries or indexes, as if 2.06 meant the same everywhere; scores only order results within one query
Changing k1 or b with a few hand-picked queries instead of a judged query set
Ignoring that idf and average length are computed per index or per shard, so shards with different data can score the same document differently
Searching a title and a body as one blob, so a body mention outranks a title match
Treating a stuffed page as solved: saturation caps the gain from repetition, but a single-word query can still reward the page that repeats it

roles.label: Shopper
roles.description: Types the query and reads the top few results.

roles.label: Index statistics
roles.description: Holds the postings and the numbers scoring needs: df per word, tf per document, document lengths.

roles.label: Scorer
roles.description: Turns those statistics into a score for each matching document.

roles.label: Page author
roles.description: Writes the pages, and some try to write for the ranking function instead of for readers.

quiz.question: A page repeats "laptop" 14 times and ranks first by plain term count. Under BM25 it falls to number 3 for the same query. Which two parts of BM25 cause that?
options: BM25 deletes any word that appears more than 5 times in a page.
Each extra occurrence adds less than the one before, and a long page gets less credit per word.
BM25 only counts the first word of each page, so repetition is invisible to it.
BM25 multiplies the score by the number of pages that contain the word.
quiz.explanation: Saturation (the k1 term) caps what repetition can earn, and length normalization (the b term) discounts a page for being longer than average. Nothing is deleted and only the first word is not used. The number of pages containing a word enters through idf, which lowers the weight of common words, not raises it.

quiz.question: A team raises k1 from 1.2 to 3 on an unchanged corpus. What changes?
options: Repeated occurrences of a word keep earning more credit for longer before they flatten out.
Long documents are punished harder, because k1 is the length setting.
Rare words stop counting for more than common words.
Every score is halved, so the order of the results stays the same.
quiz.explanation: k1 controls saturation: a higher k1 moves the ceiling from 2.20 to 4.00 and makes the curve rise for longer. Length is controlled by b, rarity by idf. The order can change, because documents with repeated words gain more than documents with single mentions.

quiz.question: An engineer sets b to 0 because "length should not matter". For the query "the laptop battery", a 40-word review that mentions the laptop and its battery once each in passing (and "the" 10 times) starts to beat a 6-word guide that is entirely about the topic. Why?
options: With b at 0 the idf of each word is reset to zero.
The review has more words, and BM25 gives a bonus per word.
Saturation stops working when b is 0, so the review's counts grow without limit.
Nothing discounts the review for being long, so its mentions count in full against the short page.
quiz.explanation: b = 0 switches length normalization off, so a long document's counts get no discount for its length (the review scores 2.38 against the guide's 1.71, where b = 0.75 gives 1.69 against 2.17), and a page that mentions the topic in passing competes with one that is all about it. Saturation and idf are separate terms and are unaffected; there is no per-word bonus.
